*Vyomavyāpi-stava* (The Hymn to the Pervader of Space).
37) The *Vyomavyāpi-stava*. The *Vyomavyāpi-stava* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka.
Accompanied by the *Laghuṭippaṇī* composed by Śrī Vedajñāna.

I bow to the elephant-faced Lord who dwells on the eternal mountain, whose trunk is agitated by the playful movement of the flowing stream of ichor trickling down His cheeks, and who brings long-lasting joy to the immovable mountain.

At the outset, by granting swift liberation, he showed his hand as one that provides refuge; here, having inspired confidence with his fearless hand, he led Satyavān across [the fire] using the fire itself as a bridge.
O Lord of the Assembly, Indra, together with a great host, [worships] that very same glorious lotus-foot of Khātuna, which was formerly made of gold.
I shall now commence a brief commentary on a single hymn to Vyomavyāpin, entitled *Śiśubodhinī*, composed by the teacher Rāmakaṇṭha.

For here, these words of praise become clear merely by showing the statements of agreement from the learned. All such statements have been cited in order within the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā* at the end of their respective components, one after another with ease, for every ten Āryā verses. (p. 2) [End of citation]
We shall demonstrate [this] later.
For now, however, for the sake of awakening the beginner, those words of praise are explained merely as an illustration of their general application, showing only the direction. Thus it is said:
In this regard, there was a preeminent teacher named Rāmakaṇṭha, whose neck was adorned with the golden garland of the Śiva-āgamas constantly held [therein];
he [resided] upon nine lotus-thrones consisting of a collection of nine locations— from the center to the northeast— situated within the nine-navelled maṇḍala praised by Rudra.

For the worship of the eighty-one constituent parts (padas) of the sovereign mantra Vyomavyāpin— which consists of three hundred and sixty-eight syllables, possesses inconceivable majesty, and serves as the instrument for destroying the entire web of bonds (pāśa).

In order that his other devotees may likewise achieve such worship, he composes a hymn of praise called the *Vyomavyāpin-stava*, consisting of individual verses (*āryā*), beginning with "That which is denoted by the syllable *Oṃ*," etc., so as to manifest the state of being a designator of Paramaśiva at every step.
By means of ninety-nine Āryā verses. Herein, this should be understood: there is a single mandala described by Ruru with nine centers;
in its middle is a lotus with a central pericarp, endowed with eight petals, and a single pedestal.

In the various directions starting from the east and ending with the northeast, there is a similar lotus in each; thus, there are nine lotus-thrones. Upon those lotus-thrones, in the nine positions consisting of the pericarp and the ends of the petals starting from the northeast, the nine words of the King of Mantras, beginning with *oṃ*, are to be placed in sequence.
Regarding the phrase "they are to be worshipped": in their worship, there is a sequential application of nine groups of ten Āryās.
Thus, on the lotus-seats starting from the east and ending in the northeast, one group of ten Āryās should be assigned to each seat. In this manner, there is the employment of ninety Āryās in total.
Thus, the nature of the nine-naveled mandala (*navanābha-maṇḍala*) is described in the *Kālottara* and other scriptures as follows:
"Now, for the purpose of the initiation of a preceptor (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), one should fashion the nine-naveled [mandala].
For all rites performed with specific desires (*kāmya*), the nine-naveled [mandala] bestows the fruit. (4)
Mataṅga said:
I shall describe another most secret [method], which is orderly, symmetrical, and auspicious.
Having divided [the space] into seven parts, one should fashion a lotus in the center.
It should be thirty-two finger-breadths in measure and well-proportioned as before;
having set aside one part in each of the eight directions in due order, (p. 4).
One should draw eight steps, each equal in measure to a central lotus,
with two parts [of space] in the four directions, resulting in eight gates as described.
One should properly fill it with dust so that it becomes beautiful;
it consists of eighty-one squares, O Lord, as seen from the description of the nine sections.
One who knows the tantras and mantras should perform worship according to the path of the teachings spoken by Śiva.
(39) Its nature is clearly stated in the *Kālottara*:
"In the center is a white lotus, and yellow in the direction to its east. (9)
In the southeast is the red-colored [lotus], with a blue lotus situated in the south;
in the southwest is the yellow-colored [lotus], and the white one is situated in the direction of Varuṇa (the west).
Smoky-grey in the northwest, red and yellow in the north,
and resembling a pearl or white in the northeast— these are the nine [colors] situated in their respective directions.
Furthermore, a ruby or even one that is reddish-white is prescribed for the rite of the ninefold sacrifice (navādhvara) belonging to Śiva himself, which pervades the sky. (12)
This is declared to be the nine-petalled [mandala] known as the Prāsāda of Śiva;
Śiva is to be worshipped in the central lotus, and the world-protectors (lokeśas) in the others.
Then, one should worship the weapons with devotion during the external rite;
he is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
In the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites, one should act for the sake of enjoyment and liberation.

Likewise, it has been stated by the Śivācāryas, O Trilocana: "In the sacred field (kṣetra) measured by seven steps, a lunar square (śaśipada) is prescribed on all sides by those who possess wisdom. (vīthī)
In the eight directions, there are lotuses, and around them, a path measuring one-sixteenth of the moon [unit];
there are eight doors situated between the lotuses by means of the remaining steps; within this is the Gātraka lotus—this is the nine-navel maṇḍala proclaimed in the venerable Mataṅga. 15½.

(6) Now, one might ask: for what purpose did the Teacher compose this hymn of praise using the term *vyomavyāpin* within mantras consisting of sixty-eight syllables, three hundred syllables, one thousand syllables, or more?

If you say this is not so, it is not; for among the seventy million great mantras (*mahāmantra*), this very *Vyomavyāpin* mantra is described in the scriptures (*āgama*) as the king of mantras (*mantrarāja*) and as possessing supreme majesty. Likewise, in the *Kālottara*, in the chapter on the path of mantras (*mantrādhva-paṭala*), its status as the king of mantras is described as follows: [The passage continues...]
O Six-faced One, listen now as I shall describe the path of mantra.
Seven thousand million, as well as one hundred thousand million, and thirty-six thousand—these have emerged from Sadyojāta. (17)
Twenty thousand crores, as well as one hundred thousand crores, and sixty-four million [verses] have emerged from Vāmadeva. (18)
O child, forty-four billion,
three million, and one hundred thousand [mantras] indeed issued forth from Aghora.
O Six-faced One, eighty-four million and four hundred thousand varieties of mantras have emerged from that Puruṣa. (20)
For thousands of millions of eons and hundreds of millions of eons,
an infinite web of mantras has issued from the mouth of Īśāna.
This collection of mantras, which emerged from the mouth of Īśāna, is extremely difficult to obtain;
for this unsurpassed king of tantras consists of eighty-one sections.
The great mantra known as Vyomavyāpin consists of three hundred and sixty syllables;
the word Vyomavyāpin arose from the head of Īśāna.
40) The mantra of eighty-one words is the most supreme among all mantras;
it consists of three hundred and sixty-six unsurpassed syllables.

O Guha, one should recite [the mantra] at the time of the secret fire-sacrifice (homakāla), at the time of bathing, at the time of consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), and indeed at the time of initiation (dīkṣā). || 25 ||

One should indeed recite [the mantra] during the Vasordhārā rite, during a conflagration of the earth, as well as for extraordinary pacificatory rites, in cases of drought, earthquakes, and indeed during all portents. (26)
By reciting this mantra once, one is liberated from bad dreams and contact with wicked people;
this is the Īśāna-mantra that has emerged as all-pervading like the sky. (27)
One should worship the crown and other ornaments with the mantras of the Īśāna-head.

The thousand-syllable mantra born from the Tatpuruṣa-face is employed for the food offering, incense, lamps, and so forth, as well as for the Tatpuruṣa-mantra itself. The ten-thousand-syllable [mantra] born from the Aghora-face [is used for the same].
The Aghora mantra is employed for the bracelets, armlets, and other ornaments. Thus, because it is born from the face of Īśāna,
because it consists of the words of the Vyomavyāpin [mantra], because it is the king of mantras, because it is suitable for worship with the crown and other regalia,
and because it generates the Īśāna mantra, it is a mantra suitable for the worship of the limbs (aṅga-pūjā) for those born from the Aghora face.

Because the Vyomavyāpin mantra, consisting of three hundred and sixty-eight syllables, is described as the most excellent among all mantras when compared to the progenitor mantras of a thousand syllables, ten thousand syllables, and a hundred million syllables.
(p. 9) Thus, Rāmakaṇṭhācārya’s engagement was for the purpose of praising that state (*tatpada*).

Since this King of Hymns (*stavarāja*) was composed in accordance with the *Raurava[-tantra]*, the author of the hymn, in reference to its recitation, [describes] the mantra further on as consisting of three hundred and sixty-eight syllables.
Thus it has been described. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the number established by the recitation in the *Kālottara* and other scriptures.
As it is said in the *Raurava*: "Now, the number of Śiva's syllables is declared to be three hundred. (28)
Sixty-eight secret mantras of Śambhu have emerged;
in the Mataṅga,
however, all eighty-one words are found together in one place.
Three hundred and sixty-eight [fingers] for Śambhu’s left side;
thus is the determination of the introductory exposition.

Thus, he first praises the manner of the hymn for the first word of this king of mantras, which pervades the sky, as follows: "Oṃkāra..."— [he praises] Śiva, who is denoted by the syllable Oṃ, who is primordial, and who is endowed with uninterrupted vision and action.
I bow to the body of the five Great Praṇavas, which bestows the highest good upon the entire world. || 29 ||
Commentary: The syntactical connection is "I bow to the primordial Śiva, who is denoted by the syllable Oṃ.
He is endowed with—that is, possessed of—the two sovereign powers consisting of knowledge and action, namely, vision and activity, which are unconditioned and uncontracted.

He whose body consists of the five *mahāpraṇavas*, which are the five *brahma-mantras*— that Śiva, the bestower of welfare upon the entire world, the whole universe, and the accomplisher of the human goals of prosperity (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*)— is [described] by the first term [of the compound]; by this, the state of one who is already liberated (*mukta-pada*) is excluded.
It is well known that this Śiva is denotable by the syllable *oṃ*; "I bow to him" means that I praise him.

Here, through the praise of Śiva, who is the denoted (*vācya*), the word *oṃ*, which is the denoter (*vācaka*), is itself praised, because of the non-difference between the denoted and the denoter. Thus, in all subsequent instances as well, [the denoter is praised] through the praise of the denoted.
The praise of the words themselves must be understood. He states the praise of the second word: "Pervading the sky" (*vyomavyāpaka*), etc.:

Salutations to that Vyomavyāpin, who pervades the sky, who is immeasurable, who is Māyā, who is the Lord (*nātha*) who destroys the bonds of Pāśupati, and who pervades [all things] with his powers. (2)

The grammatical connection is as follows: "Salutations to that Vyomavyāpin (Pervader of Space), who pervades with his powers that immeasurable, all-pervading void which is the Lord accompanied by Māyā, the Paśu, and the multitude of bonds. By means of Māyā, the individual soul (Paśu), and the mass of fetters, [He is] the Lord; "immeasurable" means devoid of limitation.
To that Śiva who pervades even that space which is all-pervasive, omnipresent, and the fifth element, the sky— since all visible objects are contained within space, its nature as fire is evident—
and who, having pervaded it, remains there through his powers (śaktis).
To that which pervades even that space—to Him who is the pervader of the sky—*namaḥ vyomavyāpine*.
By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "He pervades the sky" (*vyoma vyāpnoti*), the meaning is: *namaḥ* (salutation) to the one denoted by the term *vyomavyāpin*.
He speaks the praise of the third state with the words "tadvat" (in the same way):

"In the same way, to You whose stainless, supreme form is the all-pervading void, and whose nature is partless, and who possess omniscience and other such qualities—to You, whose form is the void, let there be salutation. (3)

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Salutation be to Him whose form is space (*vyomarūpa*), who is like that [space]—all-pervading, stainless, and whose supreme space consists of omniscience and other such qualities;
who is the supreme space of Śiva, greater than ordinary space, and partless (*niṣkala*), being devoid of parts."
To that Śiva, whose nature is omniscience and so forth, who possesses the form and body of all-creatorship, eternal contentment, awakening, and the like;
who, like space, is all-pervading, omnipresent, stainless, and pure— to you, O Vyomarūpa (Space-formed), so called by the etymological derivation "one whose form is like space."
The meaning is: "Let there be salutation."

He speaks the praise of the fourth quarter with the words "by the void" (vyomena): "Just as by the void all else—the lower principles, states of being, and worlds—is pervaded, so too is that which is called the supreme beyond the supreme; salutation to You, the all-pervasive One. (4)

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "He who is beyond the beyond, together with the sky, and all else that is beneath you—the principles (*tattva*), states of being (*bhāva*), and worlds (*bhuvana*)—that which is called Power (*śakti*); salutation to that all-pervading one.
(p. 3) "Beyond the beyond" means higher even than the highest; this is an address to Śiva.
By this [statement], it is understood that there is indeed a word "vyoman" ending in the vowel "a. This third case ending is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*);

the meaning is: "everything else, the entire universe other than [yourself], along with space (*ākāśena saha*), is pervaded by you. Because of which cause [this is so], [there are] the principles, states of being, and worlds; these are the *tattvas*.
The thirty-six categories (*bhāvas*), the fifty worlds (*bhuvanas*), and two hundred twenty-four—
these constitute that which is called *Śakti*, whose nature is Your power; because of that reason,
[salutations] to the All-pervasive One (*sarvavyāpin*), who is designated by the term "all-pervasive" according to the etymology "that which pervades everything."
The meaning is: "Salutation to you."

He speaks the praise of the fifth quarter beginning with "rāgāt": "Because of the impossibility of association with defects such as passion and the like, which have been established since beginningless time; to Him who is eternally peaceful and thus Śiva—to that Śiva, salutation! (5)

The syntactical connection is as follows: "Obeisance to that Śiva," for whom the occurrence of defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth is impossible due to his primordial, eternally established state of perpetual peace (*sadā-śāntatva*), which constitutes his nature as Śiva. For that Śiva, [passion and so forth...]

Free from defects, [He is] established from beginningless time; this is an expression emphasizing the state of being (bhāva-pradhāna-nirdeśa), meaning that because He is perfected and beginningless. Because He is eternally peaceful and gentle, there is "Śivatā," which is purity;
"Salutation to that Śiva" means salutation to Him who is denoted by the word Śiva.
He speaks the hymn of the sixth state: "Antaḥ" etc.—Salutations to that infinite Śiva, whose prior limit (pūrvakoṭi) is internal because of its primacy; for whom no birth has ever been spoken of. 6.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Salutations be to that Infinite One (*ananta*), who has no end, no prior limit (*pūrvā koṭiḥ*), and whose birth is said to be non-existent due to his primacy.
Here, "end" (*antaḥ*) refers to destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*); "prior limit" (*pūrvā koṭiḥ*) refers to antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); and "birth" (*janma*) is said to be emergence (*udbhava*).

"Devoid of beginning, middle, and end" means this. Why? Because of being "first," which signifies existing prior to all effects; the point is that such priority is not perceived in things that possess a beginning, middle, and end. Regarding "to the infinite" (*anantāya*): the word "infinite" (*ananta*) [also applies] to the beginning and the middle.
"Upalakṣukaḥ": by the etymological derivation "he for whom [limitation] does not exist," the meaning is "salutation to the one denoted by the word 'ananta' (the infinite)."

He speaks the praise of the one who has no protector (Anātha) with the verse beginning "Nātha": "Salutations to that Anātha, who is called the Protector (nātha), the Lord (svāmī), the Friend (mitra), and the Kinsman (bandhu); he who is like a father (sanāstiya) and is declared to possess eternal, universal sovereignty. (7)

The grammatical construction is as follows: "Salutations to that one who is without a protector (anātha), for whom there exists no master, friend, kinsman, or lord, because of the eternally proclaimed state of being the Lord of all. This is because Śiva possesses the quality of being the eternal Lord of all, as declared in the Śiva-āgamas.

The meaning is that he does not possess a master or the like. By the etymological derivation "one for whom masters—meaning masters and so forth—do not exist," the sense is: "Homage be to him who is denoted by the word 'anātha' (the masterless one)."

(p. 16) He speaks the hymn to the eighth state (Anāśrita): "O You who, in the performance of the work of creation and so forth, have no other assistant upon whom You depend; who are liberated and are the liberator of Śiva and others—salutations to You, even though You are Anāśrita (the Unsupported). || 8 ||

The syntactical connection is as follows: "Salutation be to that Anāśrita (the Unsupported One), by whom—being liberated himself—the one to be liberated, such as Śiva and others, is assisted in the performance of the fivefold cosmic acts beginning with creation; for no other assistant has been relied upon. By which Śiva, in the performance of the fivefold acts beginning with creation, some liberated person or other distinct from himself is not at all required as an assistant.
The meaning is: "Salutation to Him who is not dependent, who is expressed by the term 'the non-dependent state' (anāśritapada)."
943) He speaks the praise of the ninth word, beginning with "adhruvam":
"This object is for the most part unstable, yet it bestows the goals of human life; therefore, Śambhu is said here to be the stable one. Let there be salutation to that Stable One. (9)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Salutation be to that Śambhu who is said to be eternal and fixed (*dhruva*), for this object which bestows the goals of human life is generally unstable.
(p. 17) This visible object, such as a beloved woman and so forth, is that which bestows the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).

Since [this world] is generally, by certainty, unstable and perishable, for that reason, salutation to Him who is called Śambhu— the one who bestows happiness, the creator of auspiciousness (śivatā), eternal and devoid of destruction— who is described in the Śiva-āgamas; this is the meaning of "salutation to Him denoted by the word *dhruva* (the eternal)."
Now he describes the method of worshipping the nine syllables: "The group of nine syllables... etc.
This group of nine syllables, consisting of thirty-five phonemes, is to be worshipped within the nine-petalled [lotus] resembling a lotus.
It is situated upon the central pedestal (pīṭha), with its petals located in the directions starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
The grammatical connection is that these nine groups of words, consisting of thirty-five syllables each, are to be worshipped in the nine-naveled [mandala].

The meaning is that the nine words beginning with *oṃ* are to be worshipped in the nine squares of the central lotus seat, starting from the pericarp and extending to the petals ending in the northeast.
