Now, he expresses praise for the thirteenth word with "yo'sau":... [the verses follow] ... (p. 64) ...Thus ends the praise of the thirteenth word. Now, he expresses praise for the fourteen words of the central seat (*madhyapīṭha*) with fourteen *āryā* verses beginning with "yo'sau":... [the verses follow] ... (p. 65) ...Thus ends the praise of the first word. Now, he expresses praise for the second word with "yo'sau":... [the verses follow] ... (p.

Salutations to that eternal Teacher, who, through his supreme compassion for humanity, is always a trustworthy instructor of what is beneficial and so forth, by virtue of being free from all affliction.

The grammatical connection is as follows: "Salutation to that Supreme and Eternal One," who is the teacher of what is beneficial and so forth for human beings through compassion and by being free from affliction; he is one whose scripture is always authoritative (*sadāpta-śāstraḥ*), meaning he is pervaded by scriptures at all times and speaks according to reality. "Affliction" (*āmaya*) refers to passion and the like; because he is devoid of these, he teaches what is beneficial and so forth.
By the word "ityādi" (and so forth), that which is harmful is understood. The meaning is "the instructor of what is beneficial and what is harmful.
Based on the etymology from the verbal root *śās* (to instruct) in the sense of "anuśiṣṭau" (instructing), the meaning is "salutation to the one denoted by the term Śāśvata" (the Eternal).
He speaks the second verse of praise, beginning with "yoga":
"Yoga has the form of Sadāśiva, and Śakti, residing therein, performs everything;
salutation to Him whose seat is that [yoga], who is established as Taptīṭha. (12)
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "That which is the body of Sadāśiva, namely Śakti, and Yoga, situated therein, performs everything—that is his *pīṭha*;

salutation to him who is established in that *pīṭha*. Śakti, which constitutes the very body of Sadāśiva, is to be understood as the power of Yoga (*yoga-śakti*); residing there, Śiva performs everything.

Because it performs its function (*kṛtyaṃ karoti*), that body is called a "seat" (*pīṭha*). Therefore, by the etymological derivation "one who is situated on the seat of yoga" (*yogarūpe pīṭhe sthitaḥ*), the meaning is: "Salutation to the one denoted by the term *yogapīṭhasaṃsthita*."

He speaks the third verse of praise, beginning with "nityam": "Salutations eternally to You, the Yogi, whose body is said to be eternal and never subject to destruction, and who likewise possesses the powers [of Śaktis] that are eternal. (13)

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Salutation to that eternal Yogin, whose body has been described [as such], who possesses yoga at all times, and for whom there is no destruction of his powers. By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "yoga and power belong to him eternally," the meaning is: "Salutation to the one denoted by the term 'eternal Yogin'."
(p. 20) He speaks the praise of the fourth quarter, beginning with "meditation" (dhyāna):

"Meditation is the will of the mind; by that alone comes the bringing forth of all things. To you, whose meditation is for the sake of satisfaction therein and who are the very act of taking away [all else], obeisance! (14)

The grammatical construction is as follows: "Obeisance to you, the one for whom meditation is the will of the mind, by whose mere will there is the bringing forth of all things, and who exists for the sake of their satisfaction—to you, the one for whom meditation is a necklace, obeisance.
Here, "will of the mind" refers to volitions; "all tasks" refers to the bringing forth, that is, the accomplishment [of those things].

*Tṛptiḥ* means supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). By the etymological derivation "he whose [bliss] is supreme bliss through meditation alone," the meaning is: *namaḥ* (salutation) to that which is denoted by the word [Dhyānatṛpti], the recipient of the offering of meditation.

He speaks the praise of the fifth word, beginning with "mantra": "Obeisance to You, who are 'Śivāya'—that very word which, among all the words of the mantra, is remembered first by those seeking the fruit in all ritual actions. (15)

Among the mantra-words, the grammatical connection is as follows: "Salutation to him who is remembered first by those seeking results in all ritual actions with the very words *oṃ namaḥ śivāya*. At the times of commencing rites, for the sake of the attainment of results, men should first [utter] *oṃ namaḥ śivāya*.
The meaning is "salutation to the one being remembered. Through the praise of Śiva, who is the object of remembrance, the praise of the one who causes remembrance is to be understood.
He speaks the hymn of the Sixth State (Ṣaṣṭhapadastava), beginning with "Even having created":
"Even having created all beings along with their leaders and the worlds, You remain endowed with sovereignty over them; obeisance to You, the Sovereign of All. (16)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Salutations to You, the source of all, who—having created the principles (*tattvas*), the worlds (*bhuvanas*), the leaders (*nāyakas*), and all entities (*sarvabhāvas*)—are endowed with sovereignty over them.
This is because [He possesses] sovereignty over His own created manifestation (*prapañca*), which is joined with the principles, the worlds, and their presiding lords.
The meaning is: "Salutation to the one who is denoted by the word 'Lord of All'."

He speaks the seventh verse of praise, beginning with "proktaiḥ" (p. 22): "Salutations to that Śiva here, who is inseparable from the aforementioned qualities; who is designated by that term 'Śiva'; who possesses qualities; whose form is endowed with Śakti; and who is of the nature of mantra. (17)

The syntactical connection is as follows: "Salutation to that Śiva who is non-different from the aforementioned qualities, who possesses qualities (saguṇa), whose form is power (saśaktimūrti), and who is designated by the word 'Śiva' as the Mantra-form. This applies to every aspect of the nature of Śiva—whether it be the one with qualities, the one without qualities, the one whose body is power, or the one whose body is the Mantra.
The meaning is: "Salutation to the one denoted by the word 'Śiva', which is the expressive term."
He speaks the hymn of the eighth step, beginning with "īṣṭe": "He rules as Īśāna, but not by means of dharma; therefore he is Īśāna.
Salutations to you, whose head is the supreme Īśāna, upon the crown of the head and elsewhere. (18)

The grammatical construction is as follows: "Obeisance be to You, the one whose head is Īśāna"—that is, he by whose dharma He is the Lord (īśaḥ) over all, and therefore He is the Ruler (īśānaḥ), upon whose head that [Īśāna] resides from the very beginning.
This is derived through etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) as: "He upon whose head rests the dharma of Īśāna, the Lord of all lords and the cause of all."
The meaning is: "Salutation to the one denoted by the word Īśāna."
(p. 23) He states the praise of the ninth foot with the words "In that" (tasmin): "In that Śaiva knowledge, the Supreme Person alone is to be expressed;
salutation to that Face of Tatpuruṣa, whose power is like a mouth. (19)
In that Śaiva knowledge, "Tatpuruṣa" refers to the Supreme [Lord] himself, whose power (śakti) is of that same nature; the grammatical connection is:

"Salutation to Him whose face is like that [of Tatpuruṣa]," i.e., to the one with the face of Tatpuruṣa. When the word "Śaiva-jñāna" is intended by the word "tat," and the word "parama" is intended by the word "puruṣa," the term is "Tatpuruṣa."

The meaning is: "Salutation to Him who is denoted by the compound word *vaktra*," according to the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) that the speaker (*vaktra*) is that which possesses the property of the power of sound (*śabdaśakti*).
Now, he describes the manner of worship for these nine words beginning with "etad" and ending with "tatpuruṣa":
"This," etc.— this group of nine words, ending with "tatpuruṣa," is previously established upon the pedestal (pīṭha).
Then, it should be worshipped as being endowed with forty-eight syllables.

The syntactical connection is as follows: this group of nine words, beginning with *tatpuruṣa* and ending with [the final word], consisting of forty-eight syllables and situated upon the eastern pedestal (*pūrvapīṭha*), is to be worshipped.
In the nine squares of the eastern lotus-pedestal, [one should worship] the [deities] beginning with Śāśvata in the pericarp and the petals ending with Īśāna.
The meaning is that they are worthy of worship.
Now, he expresses the praise of the nine quarters of the Āgneyapīṭha with ten Āryā verses beginning with "doṣa. Therein, he states the praise of the first quarter with the verse beginning "doṣa":
"Free from defects, non-terrible, that which effects the destruction of the defects of devotees..."
That is the heart, that is the true essence; let there be salutation to that one whose heart is not terrible. || 21 ||

The grammatical construction is as follows: "Salutations to that Aghora-hṛdaya (Aghora whose heart is reality), whose true nature is the Aghora mantra, which is free from defects and which effects the destruction of the defects of devotees. That is to say, his heart, which is the very essence of reality, is the Aghora mantra—free from its own defects and the destroyer of the defects of devotees.
The meaning is: "Salutation to the one who, by etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), is denoted by the term *aghorahṛdaya*."
Salutations to you, O Vāmadeva, the secret one; you who are the left-hand [path], the extraordinary, the playful God, and the hidden one, approved by the creative power (Prasava). 22.
The grammatical connection is as follows: "Salutations to this Vāmadeva, who is charming, who is distinct, who is this playful God, who is secret, and who is approved by all emanations.
The word *deva* is derived from the verbal root *div*, meaning "to play"; thus, he is both charming (*vāma*) and a God (*deva*).
The meaning is: "O Vāmadeva, salutation to you who are denoted by the word 'guhya' (the secret) according to its etymological derivation."

He speaks the praise of the third foot, beginning with "sadyaḥ": "Obeisance to you, whose form is Sadyojāta, from whom those whose births and so forth have been destroyed instantly—that is, immediately—become liberated as soon as they are born. (23)

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Salutation to that form which is Sadyojāta," because immediately (*sadyaḥ*), that is, instantly (*jhaṭiti*), those whose birth and so forth have been destroyed—those whose forms are dance—are liberated. (46) "Instantly" is the explanation of *sadyaḥ*, and "whose birth and so forth have been destroyed" is the explanation of *ajātāḥ*.

Regarding the explanation of the term *mūrti*: "the human forms" (*nṛmūrtayaḥ*). Thus, by the etymology "that from which the forms are suddenly born" (*sadyo 'jātā mūrtayo yasmāt*), the meaning is: "salutation to the one denoted by the term *sadyojātamūrti*."
(p. 26) He speaks the praise of the fourth quarter with "Om": "In the word 'Om', it indeed indicates a real identity (*aikya*) in its primary denotation (*vācye*);
this Śiva is entirely non-different even from his partless aspect (*niṣkala*). (24)

Here, although "Oṃ" should have been stated first, [the author] indicates the reality: "To you, who are this Śiva—both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*), and thus non-different"—this is the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*). Nevertheless, the construction is "Oṃ, salutation to you. In this teaching of Śiva, the word "Oṃ" stands at the beginning.
It should be stated that first, oneness is characterized because both the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*)—namely, the two *om* sounds—are identical;
therefore, the form of *oṃ* is indeed non-different from both the manifest (*sakala*) and the unmanifest (*niṣkala*).
Furthermore, for this reason as well—this is the meaning of "also"—there is an address by means of these two reasons: "O you whose form is the syllable *oṃ*."
This is the meaning; "salutation to you" is the meaning.

(p. 27) He speaks the praise of the fifth word, beginning with "guhyā" (the secret ones): "Homage be to the one who is more secret than even those secrets—the secrets being those things unseen by others, as well as those to be concealed from the bound souls (paśus), such as Māyā and the rest; [homage] to him who is to be attained in solitude. (25)

The meaning is as follows: cattle, horses, and other such objects, as well as matters that are secret (*guhya*) and to be concealed (*gopya*) from others who have not perceived them—to that which is more secret than even those secrets, to be attained in solitude, "salutation be unto You. The explanation of the word *guhya* is "to be concealed," meaning not seen by others; the reason for its being concealed is provided. The explanation of the word *atiguhyam* (the most secret) is as follows:
"To be attained in secret" means that which is inaccessible to meditations;
thus, by the compound *guhyātiguhyāya* (meaning "more secret than secrets"), the sense is: salutation to Him who is designated by that term through a genitive Tatpuruṣa compound.
He speaks the hymn in six feet, beginning with "eka":

Salutations to Him who, for the sake of the single human form, destroys Māyā in every way; yet, for the sake of the liberation from worldly existence of others, He is its protector—salutations to that Protector of protectors. (26)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Salutation be to that Protector (*goptṛ*), who, while by no means destroying *māyā*—the cause of the single form of the Person (*nṛmūrti*)—rather protects it for the sake of the worldly existence (*bhava*) of others.
Even when one [person] is liberated, there remains the *bhava*, which is *saṃsāra*; thus, he is the protector of *māyā* for the sake of the *saṃsāra* of others.
The meaning is: "Salutation to the one who is designated by the word 'Protector' (goptṛ) through conceptual construction."

He speaks the seventh verse of praise, beginning with "muktiṃ": "Salutations also to You, O Nidhana (the Destroyer), who, while effecting the liberation of the person, brings about the destruction of that cycle of transmigration along with its effects, such as the body and the organs. || 27 ||

(47) The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Obeisance to You, the Nidhana, who brings about the liberation of the person (*pums*) and brings about the destruction (*nidhana*) of that cycle of worldly existence consisting of the body, the organs, and so forth. Because he brings about the destruction of the body, organs, and so forth—which constitute the form of worldly existence for the sake of delusion—he is indeed the "Nidhana-maker" (*nidhanakara*), and thus [is called] "Nidhana."
The meaning is: "Salutation to Him who is denoted by the word 'Nidhana' through conceptual construction."
He speaks the hymn to the eighth state (aṣṭamapadastava), beginning with "sarva":
(29) All the millions of vidyās and mantras, and the seven lords beginning with Ananta—salutations to that Lord of all Vidyās from whom they arise. || 28 ||

The grammatical construction is as follows: "Salutation to that Lord of All Vidyās, from whom all seventy million mantras and the infinite Vidyās beginning with Ananta arise. Alternatively, by the etymology "he who is the Lord (adhipa) of all Vidyās," salutation is offered to the one denoted by the term "Lord of All Vidyās" (sarvavidyādhipa).
This is the meaning.
He speaks the hymn of the ninth quarter, beginning with "jyotiḥ":
"That light which previously manifested the entire form of men—that very light by which one is liberated;
salutations also to You, who are of the nature of that light, through both consciousness and activity regarding all objects. (29)

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Salutations to You, who are of the nature of light (*jyotīrūpa*), who previously [in the state of bondage] was the entire light of men, but in liberation manifests all objects through consciousness and activity.
By the etymological derivation that "He who manifests (*rūpayati*)—that is, reveals—the light," salutations to You, who are denoted by the term *jyotīrūpa*.
This is the meaning.
(p. 30) Now, he describes the procedure for the worship of these nine words, beginning with "this group of nine words":
"They say this is the group of nine words, situated sequentially upon the Āgneya seat;
endowed with forty-eight syllables, it is to be worshipped as before. (30)

The grammatical connection is as follows: this group of nine words, consisting of forty-eight syllables and situated upon the Āgneya seat, is to be worshipped in sequence as previously described. The meaning here is that on this seat, the nine words beginning with Aghorahṛdaya are to be worshipped.

Now he speaks the praise of the first quarter [of the verse], beginning with "parameśā": "O Supreme Lord, salutation to You, the highest, who, through the act of making them equal, stands beyond those previously mentioned—the Parameśas and the Vidyeśas. (31)

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: "Salutation to that Supreme Lord (parameśvara), who is beyond those Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) previously mentioned—who are themselves supreme lords (parameśas) due to their own state of equality.
He is called the "Supreme Lord" (parameśvara) by the etymological derivation meaning "one who is beyond (para) the supreme lords (parameśvaras)," such as Ananta and the others.
The meaning is: "Salutation to Him who is denoted by the supreme term."
(p. 31) He speaks the praise of the second quarter [of the mantra] with the words "like a bound soul" (paśuvat):
"The intellectual consciousness (*bauddhī cetanā*) of one who is like a bound soul (*paśu*) is indeed possessed of hatred and other such afflictions;
but the liberated one is like Śiva. O Consciousness, you were neither unconscious nor conscious [in that state]. Salutations to you! (32)

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Obeisance to You, who are both non-conscious (*acetana*) and conscious (*cetana*); who, like a bound soul (*paśu*), possess consciousness associated with hatred and the like, yet for whom there is no [ordinary] mental consciousness (*bauddhī cetanā*); and who, like the liberated Śiva, possess no [such] consciousness. One whose animal-like consciousness does not exist is "non-conscious" (*acetana*). One whose liberated consciousness does not exist is also "non-conscious" (*acetana*). (48)
The meaning is: "Salutation to that which, through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), is denoted by the words 'insentient' (*acetana*) and 'sentient' (*cetana*)."

He speaks the third verse of praise beginning with "niṣkala": Obeisance to Him whose form is the space of His own manifestation, known as both partless (niṣkala) and with parts (sakala); for whom there is no fixed limitation such as pervasion and the like—obeisance to that Space! (33)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Obeisance to You, whose form is called *sakala* (manifest), yet which, like the *niṣkala* (unmanifest), is fixed in the sky (*vyoman*) by its very nature of pervasion and so forth; for the sake of certainty, there is a double mention [of *vyoma*]. (p. 32) Since the word *vyoma* is eternally neuter, it is [contrasted] with the word *mūrti*, which is feminine.
The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not untenable; by the double expression "this space, this space," the meaning is: "Obeisance to that which is denoted by the word 'space'."
He speaks the praise of the fourth quarter with the words "tadvat" (in the same way):
"In the same way, Your form pervades all objects; there is no non-pervasion.
As previously stated, salutations to You, who are both pervasive and yet non-pervasive."
And to You, whose form likewise pervades all objects—just like space—and who, unlike [ordinary beings], were not previously non-pervasive;

O Pervader of the Pervasive One, salutations to You! The meaning is that, just like space, [Your form] is pervasive. Here, because of the rule that "it is indeed pervasive and not non-pervasive," salutations are offered to the one denoted by the term "Pervader of the Pervasive."
This is the meaning.
He speaks the praise of the fifth word, beginning with "varṇa" (p. 33):
"Indeed, form consists of the arrangement of phonemes together with its essence and so forth within the body of a bound soul (paśu).
But salutations to You, O Formless One, who possess no form whatsoever in that [bound] body. (35)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Obeisance to You, in whose form—consisting of animal bodies—the arrangement of colors and that which is accompanied by tastes and so forth do not exist. Here, "color" (*varṇa*) refers to [castes] such as Brahminhood;
"arrangement" (*racanā*) refers to a particular disposition of limbs; and "tastes and so forth" (*rasādi*) refers to sweet flavors, fragrances, and the like. Furthermore, it consists of color.

Neither form consisting of configuration nor form itself exists; the meaning is: "Obeisance to that which is designated by the term 'formless' through conceptual construction. He states the first line of the sixth verse: "First," etc.
O You whose form is the first among those expanding [forms], and who are indeed joined with the second and the rest;
O You whose form is that which is to be impelled by the first—let the first [obeisance] be to You; salutations to Him! 36.
Because she, being the first and foremost of all forms, having become the primary among the primary, is indeed joined with the second and so forth— therefore, the words "she is the first,
the primary" are to be supplied [to the text], she whose form is the first and is unimpelled.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Obeisance be to You, who are the first [state] together with the second and so forth.
The intended meaning is that although there is a distinction between the states of first and second, this is not a distinction of states in Śiva’s form (*mūrti*), because it is eternal.
(p. 34) He speaks the praise of the seventh step, beginning with "sarva":

"O You whose form is such that even omniscience itself is not distinct from Your splendor within Your body; since all other [splendors] have been previously negated, salutations to You, the Splendor of Splendors. (37)

(49) For one whose form is that [light], omniscience is indeed light as its very nature; otherwise, how could it be anything else? Because of the prior negation. The grammatical connection is: "O Light, salutation be to you, the Light. In the phrase "formless" (*arūpī*), there is a negation of form; this is the "prior negation," because of the restrictive rule that "light alone is the form."
The meaning is: "Salutation to the one denoted by the word 'Tejas' (Splendor) through its twofold nature."
He speaks the eighth verse of praise, beginning with "Jyotiḥ":

"Jyotis (Light) is the agent of all actions, such as the burning away of forms, by way of metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā). And that very Jyotis belongs to You in Your form; salutations be to You, that Jyotis. (38)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Salutation be to You, whose form even that [reality] which performs all actions—such as burning and so forth—by way of being characterized as an agent, is of the nature of light (*jyotīrūpa*). Here, because the word *jyotis* implies restriction through the sense of the particle *eva*, the meaning is:
"Salutation to the one denoted by the term *jyotir-jyotis*," due to the repetition of the word.
He speaks the praise of the ninth state with the words "That" (tat):
"That which is the nature of the light of the sun, moon, and fire-gem is indeed not anything to be conceptualized;
yet it is eternally pure for You. Salutation to that whose very essence is such. (39)

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "O Formless One (*arūpa*), salutations be to You, whose stainless form is never to be conceptualized—that which is always to be conceptualized as some kind of radiant form consisting of the sun, the moon, and fire. Here, *śikhī* means fire; [the phrase refers to] a form consisting of the energy of semen, lightning, and so forth.
The impure [self] never shines because of its inherent impossibility; however, the splendor of Śiva shines precisely because impurity is impossible for it.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Obeisance to the one denoted by the term 'formless' (arūpa-pada), by virtue of being devoid of the nature of impurity."

(p. 36) Now, he describes the manner of worshipping these nine words with the verse beginning "rurugītā": "This group of nine words, sung by Ruru, ending with the word *rūpa*, located in the Southern Seat (dakṣiṇapīṭha), is to be worshipped; it consists of forty-five syllables. (40)
The *rurugītā* is the final form located at the southern seat (*dakṣiṇapīṭha*), consisting of forty-five syllables; the syntactical connection is that these nine words are then to be worshipped.
The meaning is that in this seat, the nine words beginning with *parā* are to be worshipped by the Supreme Lord.
He describes the praise of the station (*pada*) of Nairṛta with nine Āryā verses beginning with "of Agni" (*agner*).
Therein, he first states the nature of the station: "This and another [station] is characterized by the fire of the time of destruction, like the fuel of Agni."
O Agni, salutations to you, whose light is the cause for burning away all impurities.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "O Anagni, salutations to You, who possess a light that is distinct from fire characterized by fuel, lightning, and the fire of cosmic destruction, and which is the cause of burning all impurities.
By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "he for whom no other fire exists apart from His own self-luminous form," [He] is the one denoted by the term *Anagni*.
The meaning is "namas."

He speaks the praise of the second quarter [of the verse] with the word "tat": "Salutation to that Light which is distinct from the light of the *pudgala*—which, like smoke arising from passion, hatred, and so forth, causes the agitation of consciousness—and which is itself free from smoke. (42)

(50) The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "O You whose light is different from that light which possesses smoke—that light consisting of passion, hatred, and so forth, arising from the agitation of consciousness (*cit*), and even from the light belonging to the person (*pudgala*)—to You, O Smokeless One (*adhūma*), let there be homage.
By the etymological derivation "that which has no light," the meaning is: "homage to the one denoted by the term *adhūma*."
He speaks the praise of the third quarter with the words "tadvat" (in the same way):
"In the same way, because that light associated with ash is produced by human agency;
but salutations to You, whose other light for all purposes is free from ash. (43)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Obeisance to You, O Abhasman (Ashless One), who are other than that light which, though described by You as having all things as its object, is like ash because it is insubstantial and produced by human agency. By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that for which no ash-like light exists," obeisance is paid to the one denoted by the term *abhasman*.
This is the meaning.
He speaks the praise of the fourth quarter with the words "That" (tat):
"That form, which is of the nature of that light, is by its very essence pure;
it is the cause of all auspiciousness. Salutations to that beginningless one, O Anādeta! (44)

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "O Anādi (Beginningless One), let there be salutation (*namaḥ*) to You, whose form—that light-form which is pure by its very nature—is the cause of all prosperity and is beginningless.
Because the form of Śiva is beginningless, and because Śiva himself is beginningless, salutation is offered to the one denoted by the term "Anādi."
This is the meaning.
He speaks the praise of the fifth word, beginning with "nāpuruṣa":
"He indeed nourishes the triad of non-men—Hara, Hari, and the Lotus-born;
he who is 'Na', 'Na', 'Na' when spoken by a woman as her very self—to him, salutations! (45)

(39) No person other than the triad consisting of Hara, Hari, and the Lotus-born (Brahmā) can indeed nourish [this teaching]; therefore, the grammatical connection is: "Salutation to him who, in this teaching, is said to be the one whose essence is the triad, namely Nā, Nā, Nā.
Because he is the designator of the three—Hara, Hari, and Brahmā, or of the three types of persons—he is expressed as Nā, Nā, Nā.
The meaning is: "Salutation to the one expressed by the word."

He speaks the hymn of the sixth word, beginning with *saṃhāra*: "O You by whom the triad [of worlds] is shaken during the withdrawal through the function of the qualities—that You who are signified here by the three *dhū* syllables, salutations be to You as well. (46)

The syntactical connection is as follows: "Obeisance be to You," who—by reason of the fact that Your own triad functions in the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra)—are expressed by the three syllables *dhū-kā-ra*, shaking [the world] by means of the metaphorical function (*guṇavṛtti*) based on the sense of "shaking" (*kaṃpana*). This is because such shaking occurs during the cosmic dissolutions (*pralaya*).

The meaning is: "Obeisance to him who is denoted by the words *dhū dhū dhū*, which signify the three types of dissolution (*pralaya*) that are easily accomplished, provided that the word *kaṃpana* functions as an indicator (*lakṣaka*) for withdrawal (*saṃhāra*)."
He speaks the seventh verse of praise, beginning with "stutiḥ": (p.

40) "Oṃ bhūḥ! Salutation to You!"—this [mantra] which, having embraced the unreal object in the form of praise by saying "This is not so," is uttered with mantra-words of true meaning, namely "Oṃ bhūḥ. || 47 ||

This collection of mantras recited by people in the world, which consists of hymns of praise, is not [itself] the ultimate reality; rather, one should address that Śiva—who is expressed by the words of mantra whose meanings are true—by embracing him with "Oṃ Bhūḥ. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Oṃ Bhūḥ, let there be salutation (*namaḥ*) to You, that Śiva who is spoken of through the mantra-words whose meanings are true. This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*). Oṃ.

By the word *śiva*, the world (*bhūr-loka*) is denoted; through the mantra *oṃ bhūḥ*, the non-difference between the Lord and the world is manifested. Consequently, the doubt regarding the unreality of the meaning of those mantras that describe the worlds—which is raised by the Vedāntins—is dispelled, because the world is established as real.
Because existence arises from the description of non-difference from Śiva, for this very reason all mantras have true meaning;
thus, the meaning is: "Obeisance to the one denoted by the word Bhūḥ, [accompanied by] Oṃ," which has as its result the realization that all mantras are indeed true in their referents.
He speaks the hymn of the eighth step: "Oṃ.

"Oṃ! To that Lord of the Earth (Bhū), who is the essence of the world along with all its constituent elements and states of being—even he who is described here as 'Oṃ-Bhū'—to him let there be salutation! (48)

The grammatical connection is as follows: "Oṃ" refers to this teaching; "Oṃ" is that which is called the Lord (Īśa) of all that exists in the world, including the principles of existence (tattva-bhāva) and so forth;

he alone is declared to be the entirety of the universe; and he is called "Oṃ Bhuvaḥ. Therefore, the meaning is: "Salutation be to him, Oṃ! The term "Oṃ Bhuvaḥ" conveys the non-difference between the Lord and the world of beings (Bhuvarloka).
The meaning is: "Salutation to that which is denoted by the word."

The ninth syllable is "om," which expresses supreme love; "sva" signifies that whose nature is supreme bliss; "ri" is said to be its primary form; "ta" is the created; "ka" is "hmoṃ"; and "svariti" is thus—salutations be to You! 49.

*Oṃ* is supreme joy; *svaḥ* is indeed of the nature of supreme bliss. Thus, the constructed form (*kṛtakaṃ rūpam*) is one whose form consists of supreme joy and the aspect of supreme bliss—namely, that which is expressed as *oṃ svaḥ*. To You, who are thus described, let there be obeisance. *Oṃ svaḥ* is the object of supreme love and the indicator of supreme bliss.
The meaning is: "Salutation to the one denoted by the word."

(p. 42) He describes the manner of worshipping these words with the following nine-word [mantra]: "This nine-word [mantra], sung thus by Ruru, is always to be worshipped upon the Navanābha seat in the southwest (naiṛta), joined with twenty-five syllables. (50)

The grammatical connection is as follows: this group of nine words, consisting of twenty-five syllables, sung by Ruru, is always to be worshipped in the seat of Nairṛta within the nine-naveled [maṇḍala]. The meaning is that in the seat of Nairṛta, the nine words beginning with "anagna" are to be worshipped.

He speaks the praise of the nine places (*padanavaka*) of the Western Seat (*paścimapīṭha*) with these nine Āryā verses beginning with "Śambhu. Therein, he first states the praise of the first place with the words "Śambhu":
"Śambhu is proclaimed to be without end through the flow of the wheel of Māyā; however..."
Salutations to You, who are immutable; salutations to that imperishable one through the destruction [of all things].

That Śambhu, by virtue of the flow of the wheel of *māyā*—and because that *māyā*, as well as the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), is beginningless and thus flows as a cause—is its creator and is without end; for "end" (*nidhana*) means destruction, and he is devoid of that, being imperishable.
This is because, in the absence of a creator, the continuity of the flow would be untenable.

Furthermore, by virtue of being immutable (*kūṭastha*), You are "without end" (*anidhana*); because the characteristic of the immutable is changelessness, You are devoid of destruction. (52) The grammatical connection is: "Obeisance be to You, the one without end, the endless one (*anidhanānidhana*)," since You are devoid of destruction in both ways.
The meaning is: "Salutation to the one who is expressed by the words 'without end' and 'endless'."
He speaks the praise of the second word, beginning with *nidhana*:
"Salutation to that Śiva from whom the *nidhanodbhava* and other [rituals] arise for Vīrabhadra and the others; salutation to him who is the Lord within the womb of Māyā. (52)

The meaning is that from Śiva, the destruction, emergence, and so forth—namely, dissolution and creation—of those headed by Vīrabhadra, who are the lords within the womb of Māyā, come to pass; therefore, the syntactical connection is: "O Nidhanodbhava (Source of Destruction), salutations be to You. [This refers to] Vīrabhadra and the others.
The meaning is: "Salutation to Him who is designated by the term Nidhanodbhava, because He is the agent of the arising from destruction."
He speaks the praise of the third state: "Aśiva" (p. 44).

Obeisance be to that Śiva, who, though not Śiva [in the ordinary sense], becomes Śiva by virtue of being the state of Śiva; he who manifests that which is the nature of karma—purely inauspicious like a guru—[as the auspicious]. 53.
He who is not Śiva is Aśiva; because he bestows what is inauspicious, he manifests only that which is unwholesome. Conversely, he who is not Aśiva is Śiva;
because he bestows what is auspicious, he manifests only that which is wholesome in the form of power (Śakti). For that reason, O Śiva, to him—

The grammatical connection is "let there be salutation" (namo'stu). The meaning is: "Salutation to Him who is denoted by the word Śiva, both by virtue of His removing what is inauspicious and by virtue of His bestowing auspiciousness."

He states the praise of the fourth quarter with the words "of all": "Generating for everyone, at all times, all that—everywhere—the fruit of the cause of action; he who is called 'All' (Sarva), yet is not 'all' (asarva)—salutation to him. (54)

For all people, at all times, in every place, and in every respect— meaning that which is entirely produced by karma, having karma as its cause and karma as its origin— that which generates the fruit, for that reason, O Śarva, to him who is described as "all" in this teaching of Śiva, to you, O Śarva, obeisance!
This is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*).
The meaning is: "Obeisance to Him who is denoted by the word 'all' because He bestows all fruits."

He speaks the praise of the fifth foot, beginning with "parama": "Salutations to You, O Supreme Self (Paramātman), who are the supreme Self and the cause that has been declared as the cause of all things that possess the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious. (55)

The grammatical connection is as follows: "Obeisance be to You, O Supreme Self (paramātman)," referring to that which has been described as both supreme and the Self, and as the cause of all causes for those things that possess the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious.
The meaning is: obeisance to the one denoted by the term *paramātman*, which signifies the most exalted Self.

He speaks the hymn in six verses beginning with "pūjyānām": "O Maheśvara, salutations to You, who are worthy of worship even by those worthy of worship—the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) headed by Ananta—and who, for the sake of liberation, bestow the state of Maheśvara. (56)

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "O Maheśvara, salutations to You, who are worthy of worship even for the Vidyeśvaras—Ananta and the others—who are themselves worthy of worship by virtue of their status as Great Lords (*maheśvara*), for the sake of liberation, that is, for the fruit of *mokṣa*.
By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "the Lord (*īśvara*) even of the great ones such as Ananta," [He] is the one denoted by the term *Maheśvara*.
The meaning is "namas."
He speaks the praise of the one who stands on the seventh step, beginning with the word "liberated":
"O Great God, salutations to You! For he is liberated even from the Śivas and is the God himself by virtue of his tranquility; since even they worship his worship, salutations to that Mahādeva. (57)

(53) He who is Śiva is liberated by virtue of being directly independent of others due to his tranquility, that is to say, because he is naturally devoid of passion and hatred; he is the God greater even than those who are liberated— for they too are liberated and they too are auspicious (śiva).
Those whose worship (*arcā*) has Śiva as its object are thus described; being such, they become his worshippers (*arcitāḥ*).

O Mahādeva, the syntactical connection is: "let there be salutation (*namaḥ*) to you. By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of "Mahādeva" as "he who is both great (*mahān*) and a god (*deva*)," the meaning is: "salutation to him who is denoted by the term Mahādeva."

(p. 47) He speaks the praise of the eighth state, beginning with "paśu": "O Lord of Existence, obeisance be to You, who are the independent Īśvara; by whose true being the bonds of the bound souls (paśu-pāśa)—consisting of the bound souls, the enjoyers, and the objects of enjoyment—are said to exist. (58)

The meaning is: "O Lord of True Being (Sadbhāveśvara), salutations to You—who are described as independent in the Śiva-śāstra with perfect truthfulness, whereas [the nature of] the bound souls (paśu) has been stated by those at the periphery [of knowledge] in the Paśu-pāśa [texts], in the Paśu-draṣṭṛ [works], and in the Paśu-śāstras. This is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*).

In the Śiva-śāstra, Īśvara is described as "Sadbhāva" (Being); thus, by means of a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopa*), the meaning is: "Salutation to the one denoted by the term Sadbhāveśvara."

He speaks the hymn of the ninth foot beginning with "sarva": Salutations to that Great Splendor, whose body is the auspicious Sādāśiva, who performs all purposes, whose great majesty is as previously described, and who is forever invincible. (59)

The grammatical construction is as follows: "Obeisance to You, O Mahātejas (of Great Splendor)," referring to Him whose body is Sādāśiva, who accomplishes all purposes, and who is the great splendor previously described, forever invincible.
The term *mahātejas* is derived through the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) of one who possesses great splendor (*mahat tejaḥ yasya saḥ mahātejāḥ*).
The meaning is: "Salutation to Vācya."

Now he describes the manner of worshipping these nine words with the verse beginning "in the western": "This aforementioned group of nine words is to be worshipped in the western seat according to the stated sequence, joined with thirty-seven syllables, always within the center of the nine [petals]. (60)

The grammatical connection is as follows: this set of nine words, consisting of thirty-seven syllables, is to be worshipped at all times on the western pedestal (pīṭha) of the nine-naved [mandala] according to the aforementioned sequence. The meaning is that on the western pedestal, the nine words beginning with *anidhanānidhana* are to be worshipped.
He speaks the praise of the nine seats (pīṭhas) of Vāyu with nine Āryā verses, beginning with "yogā. Therein, he states the praise of the first seat as follows:
"Yoga" means those whose bodies have been liberated; they are said to be Sādāśivas, and Śiva is their [goal].
O Lord, you who are the progenitor like a father through your mastery of yoga—homage be to you! (51)

"Those whose bodies are liberated are Sadāśivas. This means that the *paśu-sadāśivas* are indeed *sadāśivas*. The suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (*svarthe*). The meaning is that because the *paśu-sadāśivas*, who consist of the form of *vijñānakala*, are liberated from all bonds, they possess "liberated bodies. [They are] the *yogas*.

Thus it has been said: Śiva is their sovereign, their father, and their capable lord. The syntactical connection is: "O Lord of Yoga, let there be salutation to You. By the etymology "the lord of yogas" (yogānām adhipaḥ), the meaning is: "salutation to the one denoted by the term 'Lord of Yoga'."
He speaks the praise of the second quarter with the words "by the gurus":
"Salutation to him who, through fear and other such motives, requests the gurus for the appearance of the maṇḍala during initiation;
or [salutation] to him who says 'Release, release! to devoted and true disciples. (54) 62.
The one who, out of fear during initiation, is entreated by the gurus—the disciples who are terrified and distressed—to "release, release" the devoted and excellent disciples;
to him, [O Lord], let there be obeisance. This is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). He is the one who establishes liberation from *saṃsāra*.
The meaning is: "Homage" is for the sake of awakening to the word *muñca-muñca* (release-release).

He speaks the praise of the third foot, beginning with "madhnāti": "Obeisance to that first [Lord] who, presiding over the gurus through the initiations, churns away the fetters and other bonds; may He be the foremost for those persons whose impurities have been ripened. (63)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "O First One, O First One, let there be salutation to You, who, having presided over the gurus after this prayer, churns [the bonds] by means of initiations for those men whose impurities have ripened. He is called "First" because of His being the first due to the churning of the fetters (*pāśa*) according to the rule; hence the repetition.
The meaning is: "Salutation to the one denoted by the first word."

He speaks the praise of the fourth quarter with the words "puṃsa" (of the person): "Salutations to that Śarva, who, abiding in the Guru, chooses those persons who have sought refuge out of fear of bondage, by virtue of his acceptance of initiation; salutations to him. (64)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "O Śarva, let there be salutation to You, who, having become established in a guru and having accepted initiation, chooses that man who has sought refuge from the fear of bondage."

The word *śara* indicates refuge (*śaraṇa*), and the word *va* indicates choice (*varaṇa*). Since it indicates the choosing of a person who has obtained refuge in a definitive manner, the meaning is: "Homage to Him who is expressed by the two words *śarva-śarva* through this repetition."
He speaks the praise of the fifth state:

"Oṇu..."— "O Bhava, salutations to You, who first bestow upon men a subtle descent of power (*aṇu-śaktipāta*) through approaching a Guru and others, by means of which they become possessed of the nature of Śiva’s power. (65)

The word "yeṣām" (of whom) is to be supplied. For those persons, through approaching the Guru and others, there first occurs the "aṇu-śakti-pāta. The word "aṇu" is used here in the sense of the state [bhāva-pradhāna]; it refers to the falling away—that is, the destruction—of the "aṇu-śakti," which is the power of the impurity of limited individuality (āṇava-mala). The change of gender [in the compound] should be understood accordingly. Of them...
The grammatical connection is as follows: "O Bhavabhava, salutations to You, who exist for men by virtue of being the cause of the state of Śiva and the manifestation of their own Śiva-nature.
Because You are the cause of the destruction of the *āṇava* [impurity], the arising of the state of Śiva, and the manifestation of Śiva-nature, You are designated by the term *Bhavabhava*.
The meaning is "namas" (salutation).

(p. 52) He speaks the praise of the sixth word, beginning with "pūrvam": "Obeisance to Him who is the source of existence (Bhavodbhava), because for those beings whose bonds have been previously shattered by initiation, their state of being becomes Śiva-nature, which is the arising in that which transcends existence. || 66 ||

The grammatical construction is as follows: "O Bhavodbhava (Source of Existence), salutations to You"—this is because for those who have previously had their bonds shattered by initiation (*dīkṣā*), they become *bhavas* (liberated beings);

and since that higher abode of those *bhavas* arises precisely as a manifestation (*vivaraṇa*) of You, You are the cause thereof. [The term] *bhavodbhava* means the arising (*udbhavana*) of the *bhavas*.
The meaning is: "Salutation to Him who is designated by the term *bhavodbhava* (the source of existence) through its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*)."

He speaks the praise of the one who stands upon the seventh step, beginning with the word *jāti*: "O You who, by the very law of birth, bestow the bliss of liberation and fullness even upon these [beings], yet grant happiness to all living beings—homage be to You! (67)
To You who, by the restriction of birth—that is, by the restriction of castes such as Brahminhood and so forth—bestows this bliss of liberation;
[to You] who grant that well-known bliss of liberation its fullness, indeed the complete perfection of the bliss of liberation; and moreover, who bestow happiness upon all beings—to You, [I bow].
The grammatical connection is "let there be salutation" (namo'stu). The meaning is: "salutation to the one who is to be addressed as the bestower of happiness to all beings" (sarvabhūtasukhaprada).
He speaks the hymn to the Lord of the Eighth State (*aṣṭamapadastava*) as follows:

"Salutations to Him who, for the sake of liberation, brings about His presence everywhere at the time of initiation and so forth, and who is not subject to the influence of the northern solstice and other such factors. (68)

The grammatical connection is as follows: "Salutations to You, who grant Your presence everywhere—in all places—for the sake of liberation at the time of initiation and so forth, and who are not subject to the constraints of time such as the northern solstice. Thus, You are the one who grants Your presence in all places and at all times.
The meaning is: "Salutation to the one denoted by the term *sarvasānnidhyakara*," according to the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) [of that term].
He speaks the hymn to the Ninth State (navamapadastava), beginning with "vidye" (p. 54):

O Lord of Knowledge, by whose impulsion Brahmā and the others, along with their [limited] adjuncts, perform the acts of creation and so forth; salutations to You, who are beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, and abide in the Supreme. (69)

The grammatical connection is as follows: "Obeisance be to You, O Supreme One beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—who, by the impulsion of the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa), are the creators of the world for Brahmā and the others, including those possessed of *añjana* and those possessed of *aṇava*—and who are the Supreme. He who exists as the one transcending Brahmā and the rest.
The meaning is: "Salutation to Him who is denoted by the supreme state of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra."
He describes the mode of worship for these nine words, beginning with "vāyavyam": "On the Vāyavya seat, this group of nine words is to be worshipped as before;
moreover, it is endowed with forty-nine syllables. (70)

Now, the syntactical connection is that immediately after the worship of the western seat (pīṭha), this supreme group of nine words consisting of forty-nine syllables is to be worshipped as before. The meaning is that on the lotus-seat in the northwest, the nine words beginning with "Yogādhipa" are to be worshipped.
(p. 55) He states the praise of the nine stations of the Saumya-pīṭha with nine Āryā verses beginning with "paśu...";
therein, he first states the praise of the first station: "For he who is not seen by the vision of the bound (paśu), nor worshipped by the bound themselves and no others..."
O cause of supreme bliss, who are not worshipped by the Śaivas because they do not worship you—salutations to you!

The construction is as follows: "O Anarcitānarcita (Unhonored by the Unhonored), salutations to You, who are the cause of the highest good (*śreyaḥ-hetu*), and who, because of the non-perception of the views of the bound (*paśu-dṛṣṭi-adṛṣṭitaḥ*)—that is, due to the absence of the views of the bound—are not honored by the bound themselves, but are not unhonored by others who are Śaivas. The term *anarcitānarcita* is a compound formed by reduplication (*virukta*) based on the restrictive rule that [the lack of honor] is due to the bound alone (*paśubhireva iti niyamāt*).
The meaning is: "Salutation to the one denoted by the word."
He speaks the praise of the second quarter [of the verse] with the words "tadvat" (in the same way):

"In the same way, You are not praised by those who are bound like cattle, nor by those who are not so bound, nor by the words of mantra, nor by hymns composed by oneself; to You, who are beyond all praise—even though You are not praised—salutations!"

And likewise, "O Unpraised One" (asaṃstuta) means: O You who are not praised by those lacking cattle (apaśubhiḥ), nor by those who are not cattle (na paśubhiḥ)—that is, neither by those devoid of livestock nor by those who are themselves beasts—nor by hymns of praise, nor by verses composed by yourself, nor by the words of a formal eulogy;
to such a one as You, O Unpraised One (asaṃstuta), [I offer] my salutation (namaḥ). This is the grammatical connection.
The meaning is: "Homage to the one who is expressed by words that are neither familiar nor unfamiliar."

He speaks the praise of the third quarter: "O You whose invocation and so forth are said to be performed everywhere, whether [the deity] was previously established or not; O You whose special presence must be contemplated for the sake of the fruit—salutations eternally to You! (73)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Obeisance be ever to You, for whom [the rites] such as invocation (*āvāhana*)—which are to be contemplated through specific forms of presence (*sannidhi-viśeṣa*) and which have been taught for the sake of Your fruit—are prescribed everywhere. This means that for Śiva, who exists in all places and at all times, the invocation serves to bring about a specific manifestation of His presence.
And thus, by the rule of repetition, the meaning is: "Obeisance to that which was previously situated, denoted by the previously situated word."
He speaks the praise of the Fourth Foot, beginning with "sākṣāt" (p. 57):
"He perceives everything directly through his omniscience, and not by means of inference or other [inferential] methods.
Because he falls [upon us] while depending on the Witness, let there be salutation to that Witness. (74)

But to you, who— because of your omniscience— behold everything directly through immediate perception (*pratyakṣa*), yet do not behold inference and the like— which are described as "accompanied by dependence on *sākṣa*" because they depend upon the sense organs (*akṣa*) and thus involve a reliance on immediate perception (*pratyakṣa*)— to you, O Lord!

The grammatical construction is: "O Witness, O Witness, let there be salutation unto You. By the repetition of the verb "paśyati" (he sees), the meaning is: "Salutation unto Him who is denoted by the word 'Witness' (sākṣin)."

He speaks the praise of the fifth word, beginning with "sadyaḥ": "Obeisance to You, who, quickly providing the incomparable means for immediate liberation—namely, that which is called initiation—repeatedly utter 'mukta' (liberated) and 'turutu'; obeisance be to You in this manner. (75)

To you who, for the sake of immediate liberation, provide the incomparable means known as initiation (*dīkṣā*)—the word "for devotion" being understood as the ellipsis—"turu turu" [O you who grant quickly, grant quickly]! Thus addressed, the syntactical connection is: "to that You, let there be salutation.
(p. 58) The expression "known as initiation alone" is an indeclinable used in the sense of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), functioning through repetition.
The meaning is: "Homage to the one who awakens the words *turu-turu* for swift realization."
He speaks the hymn of the sixth foot, beginning with "pratīti":
"Salutation to Him who, like the sun, dispels the darkness of Māyā that falls upon the womb for every world, and who, like a firefly, removes it through initiation by means of union. (76)

O Patañga, O Patañga, salutations to You who, falling like the sun upon every world, remove the darkness of illusion (*māyā*)— which is of the nature of darkness— from men through the application of initiation (*dīkṣā*), according to the rule that the word *sārvavibhaktika* [is used] in the sense of "from."

The grammatical connection is "let there be salutation" (*namo'stu*). Because the particle *ca* (and) has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva* (only), a restriction is implied; thus, by the interpretation that "he takes away" (*harati*) means "he causes to fall" (*pātayan*) darkness and "he drives away" (*utsārayati*), the repetition [of the word] signifies: "Salutation to the one denoted by the term *pataṅga*, *pataṅga*."
He speaks the praise of the one who stands on the seventh step (Saptamapadastava), beginning with "Piṅga":
"O Piṅga! Like fire (*vahni*), you burn away the bonds (*pāśa*) of some in every way, while for others you do so only partially; salutations be to you, O Piṅga, to that very Piṅga! (77)

The fire is tawny (*piṅga*); the fire denoted by the word "tawny" is like that—just as fire [burns], Śiva burns some bonds in every way, while he burns others not at all. This capacity to burn them all or not at all is established through the slight ripening or the excessive ripening of impurity (*mala*), just as in the case of fire.

The construction is: "O Piṅgapiṅga, let there be salutation (namo'stu). By the repetition of the word *piṅga*—which denotes fire through the description of its color that burns all things at all times—the meaning is: "Salutation to the one indicated by the word *piṅgapiṅga*."
He speaks the hymn to the eighth state (*aṣṭamapada*): "To that [state]...

"Salutations to that [state], which, through the grace of devotion to it, produces knowledge even in those who are otherwise without measureless knowledge, within their own self which has become an object of perception for them from this very moment. (78)

(57) O Knower of Knowledge! To You—who, by the cause of Your grace through Your power, produce that knowledge even in those men endowed with grace, within Your own self which is self-luminous, immeasurable, unknowable, infinite, and beyond the range of the bound and so forth—this locative case [“in”] refers to the object; indeed, the word “even” (api) has the sense of emphasis. To You, such as You are!

The construction is "namo'stu" (let there be salutation). Here too, by virtue of the rule [of interpretation], the meaning is: "salutation to that which is denoted by the word 'knowledge of knowledge'."

He speaks the hymn to the ninth state, beginning with "vikṣobhya": "O You who, having agitated the power of sound (nāda-śakti), produce sounds through the sequence of the bindu, first [uttering them] through the mouth of the Puruṣa—to You, O Sound, and to that [Puruṣa], let there be salutation, O Sound! (79)
Having agitated the power of *nāda*, which is of the nature of *kuṇḍalinī*, by means of the sequence of *bindu*— that is to say,

by the sequence beginning with *nāda* and *bindu*— she [manifests] sounds in their subtle forms as *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*, for the sake of the human goal (*pumartha*), through the mouth of the Person (*puṃvaktreṇa*).

He composes [the verse]. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Obeisance be to you, O Word of words. The meaning is: "Obeisance to Him who is denoted by the term 'Word of words' because He is the producer of sound."
He states the procedure for the worship of these nine seats with the words "this" (etad):

"This group of nine seats on the northern throne (*uttarapīṭha*), which is [to be worshipped] according to the stated recitation, is endowed with forty-eight syllables and should then be worshipped. (80)
The meaning is that the group of nine words, consisting of forty-eight syllables as counted by the *rurūkta-pāṭha*,
is to be worshipped on the northern pedestal (*uttara-pīṭha*). Here, the meaning is that the nine words beginning with *anarcita* and *anarcita* are to be worshipped in their respective order.
He expresses the praise of the nine steps of the Īśāna-pīṭha with ten Āryā verses beginning with "kurvan.
Therein, he states the praise of the first step with the verse beginning "kurvan":
"He who performs everything residing in limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is not perceived by bound souls (paśu)."
Salutations always to You because of Your extreme subtlety; salutations to that Subtle One, the most subtle. || 81 ||

The sense is that [the Lord] performs everything residing in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) by way of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*). The reason why He is not perceived by us along with the bound souls (*paśu*) is because of His extreme subtlety (*atisūkṣmatva*); therefore, the syntactical connection is:
"O Subtle One, O Subtle One, let there be salutation to You, who are eternally so. By the repetition due to the rule of grammar, it expresses extreme subtlety.
The meaning is: "Salutation to the Subtle One, who is denoted by the word 'Subtle'."

(p. 62) He speaks the praise of the second word, beginning with "mantra": "O Śiva, O Śiva, salutations to You, who are here determined as the meaning of the mantra by this word 'Śiva', and who are ever endowed with the qualities proclaimed [by it]. (82)

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "O Śiva, salutations to You, who are always engaged with the taught dharmas through the meaning of the mantra, and who are designated here in the teaching of Śiva by the term 'Śiva' due to Your constancy.
By the rule of reduplication, the meaning is: "Salutations to the one denoted by the word 'Śiva-Śiva'."
He speaks the praise of the third quarter, beginning with "Ānantyataḥ":
"Because of the infinity—that is, the vastness—of the fruits, it has not been stated [in full], but rather in brief:
'Salutation be to the Giver of All, who bestows everything desired, both supreme and non-supreme. (83)

The connection [of the meaning] is as follows: although not stated in detail due to the infinity of fruits, yet stated in brief, "Obeisance be to you always, O you who grant all that is desired, both supreme and inferior."
The meaning is: "Obeisance to the one who is designated by the term 'giver of all' (sarvada), because he gives everything."
He speaks the praise of the fourth quarter: "OṂ"—(58) "OṂ! Salutations to that Praṇava which is to be thus sought after by means of three prostrations;
salutations to Him who, being triadic in nature, effects the destruction of the threefold bondage and its effects. (84)

The syntactical connection is as follows: having performed the sacrifice with the syllable *iṣvā*, at the end, for the sake of destroying the threefold effect produced from the *āṇava* and other bonds, that which resides in the *praṇava* and is to be honored with three prostrations—to that, [the word] "namaḥ" [is applied]. It is used for the purpose of liberating one from the three bonds; thus, *oṃ*.
"Salutations, salutations, salutations"—the meaning is "salutations to the one who causes [us] to remember the state [of the Self]."
He states the praise of the fifth word as "the meaning of the mantra":
"The meaning of the mantra is the synthesis of both [mantras] through the words 'unto Śiva' (śivāya).
To that Śiva, who is the substratum even of the mantra, to You, O Śiva, be salutation."

In the word *śivāya*, through the synthesis of both the mantra and its meaning, the sense is that you are the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) which is itself Śiva; because of being that substratum, [you] are eternally the most auspicious (*sadā śreyān*).
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Salutation be to You, to that Śiva. [The phrase] "to Śiva" (*śivāya*) illuminates the meaning of the mantra.
The meaning is: "Salutation to the one who awakens through words.
He states the praise of the sixth word: "In the state of being an effect," etc.—"That which, even upon the cessation of its status as an effect, impels us toward the state of being a cause."
Without the command [of the teacher], half of that is lost; for him who knows the final part within the *praṇava*, "salutation to him. || 86 ||

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Salutation to Him who, even when the effect has ceased, does not produce [the world] as its cause without a command, and who is not joined to anything other than His own nature within the *praṇava*. Regarding the object of this joining, it is for Him who is denoted by the word *oṃ* by virtue of having the form of the *praṇava*.
The meaning is "namas" (salutation).
He speaks the praise of the seventh step with the words "tad" (that):
"And that causality of theirs is threefold, [expressed] by three salutations.
Because of the context of the three bonds, 'salutation be to You' refers to him who destroys [them]; salutation to Him. (87)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Salutations to Him who destroys the threefold causality and the offices of the three bonds of those lords; salutations to You, who are denoted by the word 'salutation' employed by the one who liberates from the three offices. (p. 65) Salutations, salutations, salutations to the one who effects liberation from the three offices.
The meaning is "salutation."

He speaks the hymn of the eighth state with the words "tadanu" and so forth: "Thereafter, the manifestation of Śiva-nature and its increase—since these two [increase] from those two [states], O Śiva, may there be double salutation to You, that [Lord] who are saluted by those two. (88)

Thereafter, following the cessation of the three bonds, the manifestation of Śiva-nature occurs. That Śiva-nature arises from that Śiva who is the efficient cause (nimitta) by means of two salutations; that is to say, because the duality increases through the intellect, that Śiva-nature becomes twofold. Having thus attained Śiva-nature, once again—
The meaning is that the state of being a bound animal (paśutva) does not exist.
He speaks the hymn of the ninth foot, beginning with "prānta":
"O Prānta, O Praṇava, O Śiva, that which has been meditated upon by you grants this desired fruit;
it bestows upon man imperishable Śiva-hood. Salutations be to You! (89)

(66) "He who is Śiva at the end of the *praṇava*," meaning Śiva in the form of the *praṇava* at the conclusion of the mantra; "when meditated upon"—that is, when prayed to—"he bestows this fruit, which is the imperishable state of Śiva for the person. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Salutations to that *praṇava*. The nature of the fruit is the word *Oṃ*.
The meaning is: "Salutation to Vācya."
Now he describes the manner of worship for these nine words and their number of syllables: "The Lord," etc.
This very group of nine words is to be worshipped on the seat in the northeast corner (īśānakoṇa-pīṭha), made manifest by thirty-three syllables according to the recitation taught by Ruru.
The syntactical connection is that these nine words, consisting of thirty-three syllables as recited according to the *Ruru-ukta* method,
are to be worshipped in the corner of the Īśāna-pīṭha. The meaning is that within this pīṭha, nine subtle-subtle (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma*) words are to be worshipped.
Thus, having composed this hymn of eighty-one verses for the Vyomavyāpin Mantrarāja,
the author reveals his own name and demonstrates that the hymn itself follows the meaning of the commentary on the Mantrarāja composed by Kheṭapāla.
He prays for the mantra, which consists of three hundred and sixty-eight syllables, to bestow its own supreme welfare:
(p. 67) "Thus, [there are] three hundred syllables together with sixty and eight added."
May that [work] by which the venerable Khedapāla explained the mantra, the Rauravabhāṣya, and the Vārtika through his words— that is,
by means of that direction of meaning— and by which Rāmakaṇṭha composed this hymn of praise, bestow upon us auspiciousness and grant us prosperity at all times. 91.

The mantra has been explained by the author of the *Rauravabhāṣyavārttika*, named Śrī Kheṭapāla, through an eightfold application. Furthermore, together with sixty syllables, there are three hundred syllables; having thus performed this praise according to that method and meaning, O Lord, [the form is derived] from the root *śubh* with the suffix *kvip* (as in the rule *kvip ca*).

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "May that which was honored (*añcita*) by Rāmakaṇṭha—who shines like a protector (*nāthavat*), according to the etymology *sati nāthavaccobhate*—be the bestower of perpetual welfare.
(p. 68) Thus, in the manner described, [this applies] to the seats of the nine lotuses (*navakamalapīṭha*) according to the sequence of the aforementioned praise.

The sense is that for those who perform the worship of the *vyomavyāpin* mantra and its constituent words, the attainment of all auspicious goals (*sarvaśreyaḥ*) comes to rest in the palm of their hand. Thus, the authoritative statements regarding the etymological explanations of the eighty-one words demonstrated in this hymn have been clearly set forth in the *Kālottara*.
For fear of excessive prolixity, this has not been written here; the statements demonstrating its true nature are shown in the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*, so let them be understood from there.
[He] dwells eternally in the south-eastern direction of the illustrious Lord of the Cloud-like Assembly.
Known as Devajñāna and Ṛṣīndra, he is renowned throughout the three worlds.
And this exposition has been uttered by one who bears that very name.
Thus ends the *Vyomavyāpi-stava* together with its brief commentary.
Salutations to the venerable gurus.
May it be auspicious!
